_what: THE ONE LIST of everything a client can do with Wingguy. Two things are generated from it by utils/wingguyCapabilities.js and there is no second copy of the words: the SHORT answer to "what can I do with Wingguy?" (wingguy_vision in services/wingguyGetStartedMcp.js) and the FULL page at knowaguy.com.au/what-wingguy-can-do (routes/marketingRoutes.js). Checked by tests/wingguy-capabilities.test.js.
_why: 9 Nov 2026: the answer a brand-new client got on onboarding day never mentioned their Linked Helper machine, still said leads arrive by copy and paste, and was missing half of what had been built since July. It was hand-written prose, so nothing made it keep up. Now a new tool cannot ship without a line here - the test fails until it has one.
_rules: Built a new tool? Add it to an item's tools here (or a new item), or to not_shown with the reason. Then run: node tests/wingguy-capabilities.test.js

say: the sentence the client types. It must already be in content/client-phrases.json when the item has tools - that is the house rule for any sentence a client is told to type, and the test enforces it.
does: what it DOES, in Guy's plain English, before what it is called. Short dash ' - ', never an em dash. Say 'instructions', never 'rules'. No praise of Wingguy's own drafting.
tools: every MCP tool that sits behind this line. The first one is the tool the say-sentence must be registered against.
needs: machine | mailbox | calendar | notes - when the client has not connected that yet, the line is still shown, marked as opening up once they do.
added: YYYY-MM-DD for a new feature. The line carries a 'New' flag for 30 days from that date, then drops it by itself.
not_shown: tools deliberately left out of the client answer (Guy-only, or the answer itself), each with the reason.

The sections ARE THE STORY (Guy, 10 Nov 2026): ten steps in the order a stranger becomes someone you know. The page shows every step's lead in full and folds the sentences under it. A new section is a new step in that story - put it where it happens, not at the end.
short (per section): one plain line - the step's summary in the chat answer and on the page's map.
start: true on the handful of lines a brand-new client should try first - they make the 'first day' strip near the foot of the page.

VOICE (Guy, 10 Nov 2026): the page is signed by Guy, so GUY NARRATES - 'I' and 'my' are Guy, and Wingguy is always named or 'it'. Never 'I' for Wingguy and never 'Guy' in the third person: 'When it moves to email, I write the email' on a page signed by Guy read as Guy writing their emails. On this page praise is 'I reckon' (Guy's call) - the tool still never praises itself, because the tool is not the one speaking.

lead: the step told by Guy, explaining its own terms the moment they appear (Linked Helper, campaign, lead, scored, note-taker, /wg) - a reader who has never heard of any of it must be able to follow.

page_questions / page_friend: the box after the ten steps (the two questions a reader is left with) and the footer line for someone who was forwarded the page. Page only - never in the chat answer. Guy narrates, same as the steps.

page_questions.q: Why not just use AI on its own?
page_questions.a: Because on its own it knows nothing about you. It doesn't know who said yes to you yesterday, what's in your diary, what you promised on Tuesday's call, or how you like to write. Wingguy is what gives your Claude all of that. The AI is the engine. Wingguy is everything it needs to know to be useful to you.

You could start. What makes it work is the things nobody thinks of until they go wrong: offering someone a time before you know which city they're in, chasing a person who already replied by email, a thank-you note that opens the same way as the last three. I've spent thousands of hours finding those and fixing them, one at a time, and I'm still at it. That's the part you don't have to do.

page_questions.q: Why Linked Helper, and not the tool someone just told me about?
page_questions.a: I get told about a new one most weeks, and plenty of them look better. I examined every possibility I could find before choosing. Most of them run your LinkedIn from their own servers, and every customer looks the same to LinkedIn - so when one gets spotted, they all do, and it's your account that goes. Linked Helper runs on a machine that is yours alone, through a real browser, one thing at a time, at a person's pace. They're obsessed with not getting you flagged. In all my time running this, I've not seen one person using it lose their account. Nobody can honestly promise zero risk, but it's the safest I could find.
page_questions.say: Why Linked Helper and not the other tools?
page_questions.say_note: the whole story, in my words.

sections.title: You choose who you want to know
sections.short: A LinkedIn search: the kind of people, the kind of job, the place.
sections.lead: It starts with a search on LinkedIn - the kind of people you want in your network, the kind of job they do, where they are. It's the one thing in this whole system only you can do, because only you know who belongs. Wingguy helps you build it.

items.say: help me work out who to search for
items.does: you work out the search together - who, what title, where - and it shows you how to set it up on LinkedIn.

items.say: Who should I be connecting with?
items.does: my answer - who is worth your network and who isn't.

sections.title: A machine invites them for you
sections.short: A computer in the cloud that I look after sends your connection requests, every day, by itself.
sections.lead: It's a computer in the cloud that I set up and look after, running software called **Linked Helper**. Every day it sends your connection request, with your note, to a few of the people from your search - up to 100 a week, spread over working hours so it looks like a real person at work. That list of people and the note it sends is your **campaign**. It runs without you. It's checked every day and backed up every night, and if LinkedIn ever signs you out you get an email. When it runs low on people, you give it a new search.

pointer.text: Why Linked Helper and not another tool? It's the safest I could find, after examining every possibility I could find.

sections.title: Everyone who says yes lands in Wingguy
sections.short: Read, scored against who you are after, best first.
sections.lead: When someone accepts, they become a **lead** - a person on your Wingguy list - without you copying or typing anything. Their profile is read and they're **scored** against who you're really after, so the best people come first and you never work through a list in the order it arrived.

sections.title: You thank them, and the conversation starts
sections.short: A note from their real profile in about thirty seconds, sounding like you.
sections.lead: This is the moment it clicks. With the Wingguy extension in your Chrome, open their LinkedIn profile, type **/wg**, and the thanks-for-connecting note is written right there - from their real profile and what they post, not a template. What would have taken you ten minutes takes about thirty seconds, and I reckon it sounds like you, not like AI. Click Insert, read it, send it. If a line isn't quite you, change it before you send - Wingguy notices what you changed and learns from it. More on that further down.

items.does: the same note from inside your Claude - off their real profile and what they post, on your instructions, never a template.

items.say: What do I say to thank someone for connecting?

sections.title: Wingguy keeps every conversation moving
sections.short: Who you owe a reply, worked out overnight, drafts ready.
sections.lead: Nobody falls through the cracks. Every night Wingguy works out who you owe something - a reply, a nudge, a promised note - and writes the drafts, so when you sit down the list is ready. The people you already know are on it too: old conversations worth picking up again are worth more than any new name.

items.does: everyone you owe something, best first, with the drafts already written. Park someone until a date, or drop them for good.
your whole history with anyone in one go - calls, emails, LinkedIn, what you agreed last time.
rebuild the list right now if a lot has changed.
the people who went quiet months ago, sorted into worth reopening and let go, with the reopening notes written.
the people you already know on LinkedIn are worth the most. Wingguy finds the old conversations worth picking up and brings you a few each day.

sections.title: When it moves to email, Wingguy writes the email
sections.short: Drafts in your own mailbox. You press send.
sections.lead: Every email goes into your own mailbox as a draft, on the right thread, links intact. Wingguy never sends - that is always you. It can read you what they wrote back and show you the whole back-and-forth with one person.

sections.title: When they want to meet, Wingguy books it
sections.short: Real free times from your diary, offered and booked.
sections.lead: It reads your real calendar, applies your hours, the gaps you like between meetings and both time zones, and offers times that actually work. When they pick one, the invite, your meeting link and the reminders all go out. Before the call, it briefs you on who you're meeting.

items.does: three real slots that suit you both - and if they sent a booking link, Wingguy reads it and finds where you overlap.
the invite, your meeting link and the reminders, all sent. Move or cancel it later just by saying so.

sections.title: After the call, the follow-up writes itself
sections.short: Every recorded call kept against the right person.
sections.lead: A note-taker is an app that records your call and writes it up. With one on the call, the write-up is filed against the right person and Wingguy writes the follow-up from what was actually said - the thing you promised, the name they mentioned, the next step you agreed. You never open a transcript. It's your data: you can see every call it holds and delete any of it.

sections.title: It gets more like you every week
sections.short: Every change you make teaches it. Less like AI, more like you.
sections.lead: This is the part that compounds. Everything above is written on your own **instructions** - how you open, what you never say, the links you like to share. So when a draft isn't quite right, you don't just fix that one message - you teach Wingguy for next time. Two ways. Quick: click Insert, change the wording in LinkedIn and send. Wingguy keeps what it wrote next to what you sent, and learns from the difference. Deliberate: tell your Claude what you want from now on, in plain English, and you see the change before it's made. Week by week it sounds less like AI and more like you. The goal is three moves - type /wg, click Insert, send - with almost nothing to change. That's where I am now.

items.does: a guided chat that turns the standard starting instructions into your voice - your angle, who you're after, how you handle a no.

items.say: Wingguy wrote this - in future I'd like
items.does: paste in a draft that wasn't quite right and finish the sentence. It changes your instructions, not just that one message.
Wingguy looks at what you keep changing in its drafts and offers to turn each pattern into an instruction.

sections.title: And my whole method is built in
sections.short: Ask how, and you get my answer in my words.
sections.lead: Wingguy doesn't only do the work - it teaches you my method as you go: what to say when someone accepts, why the second meeting is the one that matters, how to hold a steady pace. Ask and you get my answer in my words, not generic advice off the internet. What I learn with every client lands in your Wingguy too. And when an answer isn't clear, or your question isn't covered yet, I hear about it and fix it.
